Can an owner-operator deduct per diem?

In general, a self-employed truck driver who is away from home overnight for work can deduct meals and incidental expenses, either from actual receipts or with a per diem rate instead of tracking each meal. For drivers under the DOT hours-of-service rules the deductible share of meals is 80%. Every figure in this page is a starting point to verify against the current GSA and IRS notices.

A worked example

220 full days and 30 travel days away, at a default $80 a day (verify the current rate; it is higher outside the continental US). Travel days count at 75%.

220 × $80 = $17,600. 30 × $80 × 75% = $1,800. Together $19,400. At the 80% limit the per diem deduction is $15,520. If receipts total $9,000, they give $7,200, so per diem is larger here.

At $80,000 of net profit, the 15.3% × 92.35% self-employment tax falls by about $2,193, and a 22% bracket on the deduction adds roughly $3,650 more. Your numbers will differ.

What to check

  • The current rate and travel-day percentage, from the GSA and IRS notices, not from this page.
  • That you are self-employed. W-2 company drivers generally cannot deduct these as unreimbursed employee expenses, but verify; rules changed under 2025 legislation.
  • That your records of dates and places away from home are complete.
  • The Social Security wage base for the year, which caps the 12.4% part of self-employment tax.

Can an owner-operator deduct per diem?

A self-employed truck driver who is away from home overnight for work can generally deduct meals and incidental expenses, either with actual receipts or a per diem rate, subject to the 80% DOT hours-of-service limit. Verify the current rules and rates with the IRS and a tax professional.

Can a W-2 company driver deduct per diem?

Generally not as an unreimbursed employee expense, but rules changed under 2025 legislation: verify with the IRS and a tax professional before relying on any answer.

Open the calculator, replace the example with your own days and receipts, and see which is larger. Nothing is uploaded. Related: owner-operator cost per mile calculator and IFTA quarterly fuel tax calculator.

OWNER-OPERATOR PER DIEM CALCULATOR · RUNS IN YOUR BROWSER · NOTHING UPLOADED

Per diem or receipts: which meal deduction is bigger for an owner-operator?

Enter the days you were away from home, and the page works out the per diem deduction (full days plus travel days at 75%), applies the 80% DOT hours-of-service limit, compares it with the actual meal receipts you enter, shows the larger figure, and estimates the self-employment tax (15.3% × 92.35%) and income tax it saves.

Independent of the IRS, GSA and DOT. Not tax advice.

Verify every default before you rely on it

The rates and percentages below are starting points read from memory, not live figures. Verify them against the current GSA and IRS notices: the transportation-industry M&IE per diem rate (this page starts at $80/day within the continental US and $86/day outside it), the 75% travel-day share, the 80% DOT limit, and the Social Security wage base for the year. This page makes no network calls and cannot look any of them up.

Employees: W-2 company drivers generally cannot deduct meals as unreimbursed employee expenses, but verify; rules changed under 2025 legislation. This tool is for self-employed owner-operators.

Self-employment tax is 15.3% of 92.35% of net profit, with the 12.4% Social Security part stopping at the wage base. Income tax saved is your bracket times the deduction plus half the self-employment tax saved. State tax, the qualified business income deduction, additional Medicare tax and phase-outs are not modeled.

What this does and does not say

  • Per diem is days away times the M&IE rate, with travel days at 75%, then the 80% limit. Keep a log of dates and places; a per diem still needs records of when you were away.
  • Receipts are the actual meal costs, also limited to 80%, and you must be able to document them. The page shows the larger figure; whether you may use either method for your situation is a question for a tax professional.
  • Not checked: your eligibility, tax home, state rules, whether the rates here are current, and any 2025 or later legislation. W-2 company drivers: verify; rules changed under 2025 legislation.
